newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAFRICA URGED TO SEND CLOTHES CONTRABAND TO RWANDA.
newsitem.headline: SAFRICA URGED TO SEND CLOTHES CONTRABAND TO RWANDA.

text.p: Clothing and textile industry leaders have asked the South African government to protect domestic jobs and send the 1,000 tonnes of illegal imports confiscated by customs authorities to Rwanda.

Warning that a domestic auction of the goods could cost 3,000 jobs in an already vulnerable industry, Seardel Investment Corp managing director Bernard Richards told reporters a donation to refugees in Rwanda could be a public relations coup for South Africa.

"I think it's a huge opportunity for us to go out and do good in the world without putting ourselves at risk, without costing ourselves any money," said Richards, who is also chairman of the newly formed Clothing and Textile Forum.
The forum was established in June to coordinate the interests of the two industries, which have often been at loggerheads.

South Africa's clothing industry, battling illegal imports, dumping and import tariff reductions required by the World Trade Organisation, has lost an estimated 15,000 of its 170,000 formal jobs in the past year.
Richards said industry leaders resolved at the forum's first board meeting on Wednesday to urge the government to prevent the release of the stockpile onto the South African market.

"These goods pose an enormous threat to existing employment in the clothing industry," he said, adding that the goods could be worth over 200 million rand in an eight billion rand a year industry and could destroy thousands of existing jobs.
Hennie van Zyl, executive director of the Clothing Federation of South Africa, said an attempt to donate the stockpile to Angola failed earlier this year.
He said the Department of Foreign Affairs baulked at arrangements to escort the goods to the Angolan border and see them distributed as aid.
"Perhaps we were too strict, perhaps it interfered with someone else's ideas for distribution of the goods," he said.
Richards said an auction or donation of the goods, almost all from the Far East, in South Africa would flood the domestic market, which would undermine prices and production.

"We would like to suggest to our Department of Foreign Affairs that these goods be donated to Rwanda. Instead of donating guns and ammunition and troops and instruments of war, why not do the right thing.
"It solves our problem, it gets the goods out of our market, it protects our jobs and it also gives South Africa a wonderful image in the world," he said.
International aid agencies are battling to feed and cloth about 1.5 million Rwandan Hutu refugees in that country and in neighbouring Zaire and Tanzania.
About 500,000 refugees, mostly near to starving and dressed in rags, returned to Rwanda earlier this month, leaving similar numbers in each of the other countries.
